props.title: In & Out

sections.content: In & Out (1997) marked a watershed moment for LGBTQ+ representation in mainstream Hollywood comedy. Written by Paul Rudnick and directed by Frank Oz, the film cleverly used Kevin Kline's impeccable comic timing to tackle homophobia and coming out through the lens of a small-town teacher whose life unravels after a former student outs him at the Academy Awards. The film's most groundbreaking scene - the extended kiss between Kline and Tom Selleck - was revolutionary for 1997, predating similar moments in Philadelphia (1993) and Brokeback Mountain (2005) in its casual yet meaningful approach.

sections.content: The late 1990s saw a crucial shift in how Hollywood portrayed LGBTQ+ characters, moving away from tragic AIDS narratives like Longtime Companion (1989) toward more nuanced, sometimes comedic representations. The Birdcage (1996) used broad comedy to normalize gay relationships for mainstream audiences, while To Wong Foo, Thanks for Everything! Julie Newmar (1995) brought drag culture to middle America. In & Out distinguished itself by setting its story in the heartland and focusing on a beloved community member's journey to self-acceptance.

Frank Oz's direction balanced laugh-out-loud moments with genuine emotional depth, particularly in scenes between Kline and Joan Cusack, whose Oscar-nominated performance as his bewildered fiancée captured the collateral damage of living in the closet. The film's influence can be seen in later works like Love, Simon (2018) and Happiest Season (2020), which similarly use comedy to explore coming out in supposedly accepting times. sections.content: The commercial success of In & Out helped pave the way for more nuanced LGBTQ+ stories in mainstream cinema. While earlier films often relegated gay characters to sidekicks or tragic figures, movies like But I'm a Cheerleader (1999) and Saved! (2004) followed In & Out's lead in using humor to critique heteronormative expectations and religious conservatism. The film's Midwest setting was particularly significant, challenging the notion that LGBTQ+ stories only belonged in coastal urban settings.
